title: account for a mass change in an open system by identifying the gas that enters or leaves
stem: A student heats 2.00 g of magnesium ribbon strongly in an open crucible until it has all been converted to a white solid, MgO. The white solid has a mass of 3.32 g. Which statement best explains the mass change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mass is not conserved in this reaction because energy was released as heat and light.
choices.rationale: The energy released as heat and light is far too small to change the measured mass, and the law of conservation of mass holds for all chemical reactions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Magnesium atoms became heavier when they turned into Mg²⁺ ions, because an ion has more mass than its atom.
choices.rationale: An ion differs from its atom by electrons only, which have negligible mass, so the ion is no heavier.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Water vapor from the air condensed onto the hot crucible, and its mass accounts for the 1.32 g gain.
choices.rationale: The crucible is far above 100°C, so water cannot condense, and the gain matches exactly one oxygen atom per magnesium atom in MgO.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oxygen gas from the air combined with the magnesium, and the 1.32 g gain is the mass of oxygen that reacted, so the total mass of matter is conserved.
choices.rationale: Correct: 2.00 g ÷ 24.31 g/mol = 0.0823 mol Mg gives 0.0823 mol MgO = 3.32 g. The gain, 3.32 - 2.00 = 1.32 g, equals 0.0823 mol × 16.00 g/mol of oxygen atoms.

title: account for a mass change in an open system by identifying the gas that enters or leaves (variant 1)
stem: A student heats 6.18 g of green copper(II) carbonate, CuCO3, in an open crucible. It turns into black copper(II) oxide, CuO, with a mass of 3.98 g. Which statement best explains the mass decrease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A gas, CO2, formed and escaped into the air, and its mass is the 2.20 g difference.
choices.rationale: Correct: 6.18 g ÷ 123.56 g/mol = 0.0500 mol CuCO3 gives 0.0500 mol CuO = 3.98 g and 0.0500 mol CO2 = 2.20 g; 6.18 - 3.98 = 2.20 g.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mass was destroyed when the bonds in CuCO3 were broken.
choices.rationale: Breaking bonds rearranges the same atoms and does not destroy mass; the atoms that left are in the escaping gas.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The heat from the burner carried away mass equal to the 2.20 g difference.
choices.rationale: Heat is energy supplied to the sample and does not carry off matter with a mass of 2.20 g.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Copper atoms evaporated from the crucible while it was heated.
choices.rationale: Copper is not volatile at these temperatures, and the CuO left behind holds all of the original copper.

title: account for a mass change in an open system by identifying the gas that enters or leaves (variant 2)
stem: A student burns 1.12 g of iron wool in air and collects 1.60 g of rust-colored Fe2O3. Which statement is consistent with the law of conservation of mass?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The product contains 0.48 g of oxygen that came from the air, so the mass of iron plus the mass of oxygen that reacted equals the mass of Fe2O3.
choices.rationale: Correct: 1.12 g ÷ 55.85 g/mol = 0.0201 mol Fe gives 0.0100 mol Fe2O3 = 1.60 g; the oxygen is 1.60 - 1.12 = 0.48 g = 0.015 mol O2.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Iron atoms were converted into heavier atoms when the iron was heated, which raised the mass by 0.48 g.
choices.rationale: A chemical reaction does not change one element into another, so the iron atoms keep their mass.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The heat added 0.48 g of mass to the iron, which is why the product weighs more than the reactant.
choices.rationale: Heat is energy and its mass equivalent is far too small to measure, so it cannot account for 0.48 g.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Conservation of mass applies only to closed containers, so the extra 0.48 g in the open crucible is not accounted for by any reactant.
choices.rationale: Conservation of mass applies to every reaction, and in an open system the air is simply an unweighed reactant.

title: account for a mass change in an open system by identifying the gas that enters or leaves (variant 3)
stem: A student places 2.10 g of NaHCO3 and an excess of vinegar in an open flask on a balance. As the CO2 bubbles away, the balance reading falls by 1.10 g. If the same reaction were run in a sealed, rigid flask on the same balance, what change in balance reading would be observed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A decrease of 1.10 g, the same as in the open flask.
choices.rationale: In the open flask the CO2 leaves the balance, but in a sealed flask it cannot, so the reading does not drop.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A decrease of 1.10 g, because gases have no mass and the CO2 does not count.
choices.rationale: Gases are matter and have mass; the 1.10 g loss in the open flask is exactly the mass of the CO2 that escaped.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No change, because the CO2 stays inside the flask and the total mass of everything on the balance is conserved.
choices.rationale: Correct: 2.10 g ÷ 84.01 g/mol = 0.0250 mol NaHCO3 gives 0.0250 mol CO2 = 1.10 g. In a sealed flask all products remain on the balance, so the total mass is unchanged.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An increase of 1.10 g, because the trapped gas adds to the mass.
choices.rationale: The trapped CO2 came from the reactants already in the flask, so no new mass is added.

title: choose the balanced combustion equation that matches the stated products, checking every atom
stem: Ethanol, C2H5OH, burns completely in excess oxygen to form only carbon dioxide and water. Which equation, written with the smallest whole-number coefficients, correctly represents this reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: C2H5OH + 2 O2 → 2 CO + 3 H2O
choices.rationale: The equation is balanced, but CO is the product of incomplete combustion and the problem states that only CO2 and H2O form.

choices.label: B
choices.text: C2H5OH + 2 O2 → 2 CO2 + 3 H2O
choices.rationale: It forgets the oxygen atom already in ethanol, leaving 5 O atoms on the left and 7 on the right.

choices.label: C
choices.text: C2H5OH + 3 O2 → 2 CO2 + 3 H2O
choices.rationale: Correct: left side C 2, H 6, O 1 + 6 = 7; right side C 2, H 6, O 4 + 3 = 7. Balanced and the products are CO2 and H2O.

choices.label: D
choices.text: C2H5OH + 3 O2 → 2 CO2 + 3 H2O2
choices.rationale: Changing the subscript of water to make H2O2 changes the substance, and the equation still has 7 O atoms on the left and 10 on the right.

title: choose the balanced combustion equation that matches the stated products, checking every atom (variant 1)
stem: Methanol, CH3OH, burns completely in excess oxygen to form only CO2 and H2O. Which equation, written with the smallest whole-number coefficients, is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CH3OH + O2 → CO2 + 2 H2O
choices.rationale: It has 3 O atoms on the left and 4 on the right, so oxygen is not balanced.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 2 CH3OH + 2 O2 → 2 CO + 4 H2O
choices.rationale: The equation is balanced, but it produces CO, which is not the complete-combustion product stated.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 2 CH3OH + 3 O2 → 2 CO2 + 4 H2O
choices.rationale: Correct: left side C 2, H 8, O 2 + 6 = 8; right side C 2, H 8, O 4 + 4 = 8.

choices.label: D
choices.text: CH3OH + 2 O2 → CO2 + 2 H2O
choices.rationale: It counts only the oxygen from O2, forgetting the O atom in methanol, which leaves 5 O atoms on the left and 4 on the right.

title: choose the balanced combustion equation that matches the stated products, checking every atom (variant 2)
stem: Ethane, C2H6, burns completely in excess oxygen to form only CO2 and H2O. Which equation, written with the smallest whole-number coefficients, is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Carbon and hydrogen are balanced, but the right side has 7 O atoms and the left only 6.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: It is balanced, but CO is not the complete-combustion product.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Correct: left side C 4, H 12, O 14; right side C 4, H 12, O 8 + 6 = 14.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: It keeps the coefficient 7 for O2 from the doubled equation without doubling the other coefficients, leaving 14 O atoms on the left and 7 on the right.

title: choose the balanced combustion equation that matches the stated products, checking every atom (variant 3)
stem: Glucose, C6H12O6, is oxidized completely in the body to form only CO2 and H2O. Which equation, written with the smallest whole-number coefficients, is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: It doubles the water to balance hydrogen from only the glucose and gets 18 O atoms on the left and 24 on the right.

choices.label: B
choices.text: C6H12O6 + 3 O2 → 6 CO + 6 H2O
choices.rationale: It is balanced, but CO is not the stated product of complete oxidation.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: It uses too much O2, giving 24 O atoms on the left and 18 on the right.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Correct: left side C 6, H 12, O 6 + 12 = 18; right side C 6, H 12, O 12 + 6 = 18.

title: write the net ionic equation when every ion in the mixture takes part in a precipitate
stem: Aqueous Ba(OH)2 and aqueous CuSO4 are mixed. Both BaSO4 and Cu(OH)2 are insoluble in water. Which is the net ionic equation for the reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ba²⁺(aq) + SO4²⁻(aq) → BaSO4(s)
choices.rationale: It shows only one of the two precipitates, but Cu²⁺ and OH⁻ also leave the solution as Cu(OH)2.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cu²⁺(aq) + 2 OH⁻(aq) → Cu(OH)2(s)
choices.rationale: It shows only the copper(II) hydroxide, but Ba²⁺ and SO4²⁻ also leave the solution as BaSO4.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ba(OH)2(aq) + CuSO4(aq) → BaSO4(s) + Cu(OH)2(s)
choices.rationale: It is the molecular equation, which writes the soluble reactants as formula units rather than as ions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ba²⁺(aq) + 2 OH⁻(aq) + Cu²⁺(aq) + SO4²⁻(aq) → BaSO4(s) + Cu(OH)2(s)
choices.rationale: Correct: every dissolved ion forms a solid, so there are no spectator ions and all four ions appear on the left.

title: write the net ionic equation when every ion in the mixture takes part in a precipitate (variant 1)
stem: Aqueous Ba(OH)2 and aqueous Fe2(SO4)3 are mixed. Both BaSO4 and Fe(OH)3 are insoluble. Which is the net ionic equation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 3 Ba²⁺(aq) + 3 SO4²⁻(aq) → 3 BaSO4(s)
choices.rationale: It leaves out the iron(III) hydroxide precipitate, but Fe³⁺ and OH⁻ also leave solution.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ba²⁺(aq) + 2 OH⁻(aq) + Fe³⁺(aq) + SO4²⁻(aq) → BaSO4(s) + Fe(OH)3(s)
choices.rationale: It is unbalanced, with 1 Fe on the left and a charge of +1 left over instead of zero.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 3 Ba²⁺(aq) + 6 OH⁻(aq) + 2 Fe³⁺(aq) + 3 SO4²⁻(aq) → 3 BaSO4(s) + 2 Fe(OH)3(s)
choices.rationale: Correct: the ions Ba²⁺, OH⁻, Fe³⁺ and SO4²⁻ all end up in solids. Charge: left 6 + (-6) + 6 + (-6) = 0, and atoms balance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 2 Fe³⁺(aq) + 6 OH⁻(aq) → 2 Fe(OH)3(s)
choices.rationale: It leaves out the barium sulfate precipitate, although Ba²⁺ and SO4²⁻ also leave solution.

title: write the net ionic equation when every ion in the mixture takes part in a precipitate (variant 2)
stem: Aqueous Pb(NO3)2 and aqueous KI are mixed, and yellow solid PbI2 forms. KNO3 is soluble. Which is the net ionic equation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Pb²⁺(aq) + I⁻(aq) → PbI(s)
choices.rationale: Lead here is Pb²⁺, which needs two I⁻ ions to balance its charge, so the formula PbI is wrong and must be PbI2.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pb(NO3)2(aq) + 2 KI(aq) → PbI2(s) + 2 KNO3(aq)
choices.rationale: It is the molecular equation and shows no ions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pb²⁺(aq) + 2 NO3⁻(aq) + 2 K⁺(aq) + 2 I⁻(aq) → PbI2(s) + 2 K⁺(aq) + 2 NO3⁻(aq)
choices.rationale: It is the complete ionic equation, which keeps the spectator ions K⁺ and NO3⁻ on both sides.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pb²⁺(aq) + 2 I⁻(aq) → PbI2(s)
choices.rationale: Correct: K⁺ and NO3⁻ stay dissolved and are spectators; only Pb²⁺ and I⁻ combine, in a 1:2 ratio for charge balance.

title: write the net ionic equation when every ion in the mixture takes part in a precipitate (variant 3)
stem: Aqueous KI and aqueous NaNO3 are mixed. Both possible products, KNO3 and NaI, are soluble. Which statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: K⁺(aq) + NO3⁻(aq) → KNO3(s) is the net ionic equation.
choices.rationale: KNO3 is soluble, so K⁺ and NO3⁻ do not combine into a solid.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Na⁺(aq) + I⁻(aq) → NaI(s) is the net ionic equation.
choices.rationale: NaI is soluble, so Na⁺ and I⁻ stay as separate ions in solution.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A reaction occurs because the molecular equation KI + NaNO3 → KNO3 + NaI can be written.
choices.rationale: A balanced swap of partners can always be written on paper, but a reaction occurs only if something removes ions from solution.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All four ions stay dissolved and are spectators, so there is no net ionic equation.
choices.rationale: Correct: since no product is insoluble, a gas or a weak electrolyte, no ions are removed from solution.

title: write the net ionic equation for an acid-base reaction, keeping a weak acid in molecular form
stem: Aqueous acetic acid, HC2H3O2, a weak acid, is mixed with aqueous sodium hydroxide. Which is the net ionic equation for the reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: HC2H3O2(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → C2H3O2⁻(aq) + H2O(l)
choices.rationale: Correct: acetic acid is mostly molecular in water, so it is written as HC2H3O2; Na⁺ is a spectator and is omitted.

choices.label: B
choices.text: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H2O(l)
choices.rationale: It treats acetic acid as fully dissociated into H⁺, but a weak acid is mostly un-ionized and should be written as the molecule.

choices.label: C
choices.text: HC2H3O2(aq) + Na⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → Na⁺(aq) + C2H3O2⁻(aq) + H2O(l)
choices.rationale: It is the complete ionic equation, which shows the spectator ion Na⁺ on both sides.

choices.label: D
choices.text: HC2H3O2(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaC2H3O2(aq) + H2O(l)
choices.rationale: It is the molecular equation, which writes the soluble ionic compounds as formula units.

title: write the net ionic equation for an acid-base reaction, keeping a weak acid in molecular form (variant 1)
stem: Aqueous hydrofluoric acid, HF, a weak acid, is mixed with aqueous potassium hydroxide. Which is the net ionic equation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H2O(l)
choices.rationale: It treats HF as a strong acid that is fully ionized to H⁺, which it is not.

choices.label: B
choices.text: HF(aq) + K⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → K⁺(aq) + F⁻(aq) + H2O(l)
choices.rationale: It is the complete ionic equation and includes the spectator ion K⁺.

choices.label: C
choices.text: HF(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → F⁻(aq) + H2O(l)
choices.rationale: Correct: HF is a weak acid and stays as a molecule; K⁺ is a spectator.

choices.label: D
choices.text: HF(aq) + KOH(aq) → KF(aq) + H2O(l)
choices.rationale: It is the molecular equation and not a net ionic equation.

title: write the net ionic equation for an acid-base reaction, keeping a weak acid in molecular form (variant 2)
stem: Aqueous ammonia, NH3, a weak base, is mixed with aqueous hydrochloric acid. Which is the net ionic equation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H2O(l)
choices.rationale: Aqueous ammonia contains only a tiny concentration of OH⁻, and the main base species is NH3, which reacts directly with H⁺.

choices.label: B
choices.text: NH3(aq) + H⁺(aq) → NH4⁺(aq)
choices.rationale: Correct: HCl is a strong acid, so it supplies H⁺; NH3 accepts the proton to form NH4⁺; Cl⁻ is a spectator.

choices.label: C
choices.text: NH4⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → NH4Cl(s)
choices.rationale: NH4Cl is soluble, so NH4⁺ and Cl⁻ do not form a solid.

choices.label: D
choices.text: NH3(aq) + H⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → NH4⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq)
choices.rationale: It is the complete ionic equation, which keeps the spectator ion Cl⁻ on both sides.

title: write the net ionic equation for an acid-base reaction, keeping a weak acid in molecular form (variant 3)
stem: Solid Mg(OH)2, which is essentially insoluble in water, dissolves in aqueous HCl. Which is the net ionic equation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mg(OH)2(s) + 2 H⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + 2 H2O(l)
choices.rationale: Correct: the insoluble solid is written as a formula unit; Cl⁻ is a spectator; charge is +2 on both sides.

choices.label: B
choices.text: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H2O(l)
choices.rationale: It treats the Mg(OH)2 as if it were already dissolved to supply free OH⁻, but it is a solid and must be written as Mg(OH)2(s).

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mg²⁺(aq) + 2 Cl⁻(aq) → MgCl2(s)
choices.rationale: MgCl2 is soluble, so Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ remain dissolved.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mg(OH)2(s) + 2 H⁺(aq) + 2 Cl⁻(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + 2 Cl⁻(aq) + 2 H2O(l)
choices.rationale: It is the complete ionic equation and includes the spectator ion Cl⁻ on both sides.

title: draw the product mixture from a particle count using the mole ratio and conservation of atoms
stem: A particle drawing of the reactant mixture shows 3 N2 molecules and 6 H2 molecules in a sealed container. The reaction N2 + 3 H2 → 2 NH3 then goes to completion. Which description of the final mixture is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 4 NH3 molecules and 1 N2 molecule
choices.rationale: Correct: 6 H2 molecules supply 12 H atoms, enough for 4 NH3; these use 4 N atoms (2 N2), leaving 1 N2. Totals: N = 4 + 2 = 6 atoms, H = 12 atoms, as in the reactants.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 6 NH3 molecules and nothing else
choices.rationale: 6 NH3 would need 18 H atoms, but only 12 are present, and it ignores that H2 runs out first.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 6 NH3 molecules and 3 H2 molecules
choices.rationale: 6 NH3 and 3 H2 contain 24 H atoms, twice as many as were available, so atoms are not conserved.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 4 NH3 molecules and 2 N2 molecules
choices.rationale: 4 NH3 and 2 N2 contain 8 N atoms, but only 6 were present, so atoms are not conserved.

title: draw the product mixture from a particle count using the mole ratio and conservation of atoms (variant 1)
stem: A particle drawing of the reactant mixture shows 6 H2 molecules and 4 O2 molecules in a sealed container. The reaction 2 H2 + O2 → 2 H2O then goes to completion. Which description of the final mixture is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 8 H2O molecules
choices.rationale: 8 H2O would need 16 H atoms but only 12 are available, so hydrogen is limiting.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 6 H2O molecules and 1 O2 molecule
choices.rationale: Correct: 6 H2 needs 3 O2 and makes 6 H2O, leaving 4 - 3 = 1 O2. Atoms: O = 6 + 2 = 8, H = 12, as before.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 6 H2O molecules and 3 O2 molecules
choices.rationale: It makes 6 H2O but does not subtract the O2 consumed, so oxygen atoms would not be conserved (12 O instead of 8).

choices.label: D
choices.text: 6 H2O molecules and 2 O2 molecules
choices.rationale: It leaves 2 O2, giving 10 O atoms in total instead of 8, so atoms are not conserved.

title: draw the product mixture from a particle count using the mole ratio and conservation of atoms (variant 2)
stem: A particle drawing of the reactant mixture shows 3 CH4 molecules and 4 O2 molecules in a sealed container. The reaction CH4 + 2 O2 → CO2 + 2 H2O then goes to completion. Which description of the final mixture is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 2 CO2 molecules, 4 H2O molecules and 1 CH4 molecule
choices.rationale: Correct: 4 O2 reacts with 2 CH4, giving 2 CO2 and 4 H2O, leaving 1 CH4. Atoms: C = 2 + 1 = 3; H = 8 + 4 = 12; O = 4 + 4 = 8.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 3 CO2 molecules and 6 H2O molecules
choices.rationale: 3 CO2 and 6 H2O would need 12 O atoms, but only 8 are present because O2 is limiting.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 2 CO2 molecules, 4 H2O molecules and 2 CH4 molecules
choices.rationale: 2 CH4 left over would give 4 carbon atoms in total, but only 3 were present.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 2 CO2 molecules, 2 H2O molecules and 1 CH4 molecule
choices.rationale: 2 H2O gives only 8 H atoms in total, but 12 were present, so hydrogen is not conserved.

title: draw the product mixture from a particle count using the mole ratio and conservation of atoms (variant 3)
stem: A particle drawing of the reactant mixture shows 6 SO2 molecules and 5 O2 molecules in a sealed container. The reaction 2 SO2 + O2 → 2 SO3 then goes to completion. Which description of the final mixture is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 6 SO3 molecules and no other molecules
choices.rationale: This treats all the O2 as used up, but SO2 is the limiting reactant and 2 O2 remain.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 6 SO3 molecules and 4 O2 molecules
choices.rationale: 6 SO3 and 4 O2 contain 26 O atoms, but only 22 were present.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 6 SO3 molecules and 5 O2 molecules
choices.rationale: 6 SO3 and 5 O2 would mean no O2 was consumed, but 6 SO3 contain O atoms that came from it, giving 28 O atoms instead of 22.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 6 SO3 molecules and 2 O2 molecules
choices.rationale: Correct: 6 SO2 needs 3 O2 and makes 6 SO3, leaving 5 - 3 = 2 O2. Oxygen atoms: 18 + 4 = 22 = 12 + 10.

title: decide which quantities are conserved in a particle-level representation of a reaction
stem: A sealed, rigid container holds 4 H2 molecules and 2 O2 molecules. They react completely according to 2 H2 + O2 → 2 H2O. Which statement correctly compares the contents before and after the reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The total number of molecules and the total mass are the same, but the number of atoms changes.
choices.rationale: The number of molecules is not conserved, since 6 molecules form 4, and atoms are conserved instead.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The total number of molecules and the total number of atoms are the same, but the total mass changes.
choices.rationale: Mass is conserved because the number of each kind of atom is conserved, so mass does not change.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The number of molecules, the number of atoms of each element and the total mass all change because a new substance forms.
choices.rationale: Forming a new substance rearranges atoms but never changes how many atoms of each element there are or their total mass.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The total number of atoms of each element and the total mass are the same, but the number of molecules changes from 6 to 4.
choices.rationale: Correct: before, 6 molecules containing 8 H and 4 O atoms; after, 4 H2O molecules containing 8 H and 4 O atoms. The mass is the same.

title: decide which quantities are conserved in a particle-level representation of a reaction (variant 1)
stem: A rigid container at constant temperature holds 4 CO molecules and 2 O2 molecules at a pressure P0. They react completely according to 2 CO + O2 → 2 CO2. What is the pressure after the reaction, if all species are gases?

choices.label: A
choices.text: P0, because mass and atoms are conserved.
choices.rationale: Pressure depends on the number of gas molecules, which is not conserved, even though mass and atoms are.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 1.5 P0, because 4 CO2 molecules are formed from the reactants.
choices.rationale: It divides in the wrong direction, treating the number of molecules as rising from 4 to 6.

choices.label: C
choices.text: (2/3) P0, because the number of gas molecules falls from 6 to 4.
choices.rationale: Correct: before, 6 gas molecules; after, 4 CO2 molecules. At constant V and T, pressure is proportional to the number of molecules, so P = (4/6) P0.

choices.label: D
choices.text: (1/2) P0, because the 2 O2 molecules and 2 of the CO molecules disappear.
choices.rationale: After the reaction only the 4 CO2 molecules remain, so the ratio of molecules is 4 to 6, and not 1 to 2; no CO is left over because the 4 CO and 2 O2 react in exactly the 2:1 ratio.

title: decide which quantities are conserved in a particle-level representation of a reaction (variant 2)
stem: A sealed rigid container holds 6 H2O2 molecules, which decompose completely according to 2 H2O2 → 2 H2O + O2. Which statement about the contents after the reaction is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: There are 6 molecules, because the number of molecules is conserved in a reaction.
choices.rationale: The number of molecules is not conserved, since 2 H2O2 make 3 molecules.

choices.label: B
choices.text: There are 9 molecules and the total number of atoms is 24, unchanged.
choices.rationale: Correct: 6 H2O2 gives 6 H2O + 3 O2 = 9 molecules; atoms before 6 × 4 = 24; after 6 × 3 + 3 × 2 = 24.

choices.label: C
choices.text: There are 9 molecules and the total number of atoms is 30.
choices.rationale: The extra 6 atoms are counted from nothing, but atoms are conserved in a chemical reaction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: There are 12 molecules, because each H2O2 gives one H2O and one O2.
choices.rationale: Each pair of H2O2 gives two H2O and one O2, so each H2O2 gives one H2O and only half an O2.

title: decide which quantities are conserved in a particle-level representation of a reaction (variant 3)
stem: A beaker holds a solution with 5 Ag⁺, 5 NO3⁻, 3 Na⁺ and 3 Cl⁻ ions (represented as particles). AgCl is insoluble and NaNO3 is soluble. Which description of the mixture after the precipitation is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 5 AgCl(s) with 3 Na⁺ and 5 NO3⁻ in solution
choices.rationale: It forms 5 AgCl, but only 3 Cl⁻ are present, so no more than 3 can form.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 3 AgCl(s) with 2 Ag⁺, 3 Na⁺ and 5 NO3⁻ in solution
choices.rationale: Correct: only 3 Cl⁻ are available, so 3 AgCl form and 2 Ag⁺ remain. The solution has charge +2 + 3 = +5 and -5, so it is neutral.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 3 AgCl(s) with 2 Ag⁺, 3 Na⁺ and 2 NO3⁻ in solution
choices.rationale: It removes 3 nitrate ions without a reason, leaving a solution with +5 charge and only -2 charge.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 3 AgCl(s), 3 NaNO3(s), and 2 Ag⁺ and 2 NO3⁻ in solution
choices.rationale: NaNO3 is soluble and its ions are spectators, so it does not form a solid.

title: judge which observation is real evidence of a new substance
stem: A student records four separate observations. Which one is the strongest evidence that a chemical change occurred?

choices.label: A
choices.text: White crystals stirred into water disappear, and the temperature of the water drops by 3°C.
choices.rationale: Dissolving can absorb heat, but the crystals can be recovered unchanged on evaporation, so a temperature change alone does not show a new substance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A colorless liquid is heated to boiling; the vapor is condensed, and the collected liquid has the same boiling point as the original liquid.
choices.rationale: The condensed liquid has the same boiling point, which shows it is the same substance as before.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A blue solid melts to a deep blue liquid at 110°C and solidifies back to the same blue solid when cooled.
choices.rationale: A color-preserving melting and refreezing returns the identical solid, so only a change of state occurred.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A shiny gray metal ribbon burns in air with a bright white flame, leaving a white powder that is heavier than the ribbon and does not conduct electricity.
choices.rationale: Correct: only C produces a substance with properties different from the starting material (metal to nonconducting powder). A is dissolving, B is a boiling and condensing cycle, and D is melting and freezing.

title: judge which observation is real evidence of a new substance (variant 1)
stem: A student heats a white solid and records the observations below. Which observation, if made, would show that a chemical change occurred?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The heated solid releases a gas that turns limewater cloudy, and the residue has a different melting point and a lower mass than the original solid.
choices.rationale: Correct: a new gas and a residue with a different melting point show new substances formed; A, B and C each recover the same substance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The solid melts at 80°C, and the cooled liquid solidifies to a white solid that again melts at 80°C.
choices.rationale: Repeated melting at the same temperature shows the substance did not change, only its state.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The solid dissolves in water, and after the water evaporates the recovered solid has the same mass and the same melting point as before.
choices.rationale: The recovered solid has the same properties, so dissolving was physical.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The solid sublimes onto a cold surface as crystals that have the same melting point as the original solid.
choices.rationale: Sublimation is a change of state and the crystals keep their melting point, so the same substance remains.

title: judge which observation is real evidence of a new substance (variant 2)
stem: Which process involves breaking covalent bonds within molecules, and is therefore a chemical change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Heating sugar until it chars into black carbon and water vapor
choices.rationale: Correct: charring forms new substances (carbon and water) from sucrose, so covalent bonds in sucrose break. B, C and D only overcome forces between intact molecules.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dissolving sugar in water so the sucrose molecules separate from one another
choices.rationale: Dissolved sucrose molecules are still intact molecules of sucrose, held to water by intermolecular forces.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Boiling water to steam
choices.rationale: Boiling water separates intact H2O molecules without breaking O-H bonds.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Melting an ice cube
choices.rationale: Melting ice loosens hydrogen bonds between water molecules and leaves the molecules unchanged.

title: judge which observation is real evidence of a new substance (variant 3)
stem: A student tests four trials on a 5.00 g sample of a white solid with a melting point of 63°C. Which trial describes only a physical change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: After heating in a sealed tube, the mass is still 5.00 g, but the solid now melts at 120°C.
choices.rationale: The same mass but a different melting point means the solid is now a different substance, even though no gas escaped.

choices.label: B
choices.text: After dissolving the solid in water and evaporating the water, 5.00 g of white solid is recovered, and it melts at 63°C.
choices.rationale: Correct: only trial C recovers the original substance with the same mass and melting point; in A, B and D the product has a different melting point, which shows a new substance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: After heating, 1.20 g of an odorous gas is released, and the remaining solid melts at 90°C.
choices.rationale: A released gas and a residue with a different melting point indicate that new substances formed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: After mixing with a clear liquid, a bright yellow solid forms that melts at 98°C.
choices.rationale: A differently colored solid with a new melting point is a new substance formed from the mixing.

title: use energy data to tell breaking intermolecular forces from breaking covalent bonds
stem: The energy needed to vaporize 1 mol of H2O(l) at 25°C is 44 kJ. The energy needed to decompose 1 mol of H2O(g) into H2(g) and 1/2 O2(g) is 242 kJ. Which statement best interprets these data?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Vaporization breaks some of the O-H bonds in water, but decomposition breaks every one of them, which takes more energy.
choices.rationale: Vaporization leaves each H2O molecule intact, with all of its O-H bonds unbroken, since only attractions between molecules are overcome.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Vaporization only overcomes intermolecular forces between intact molecules, while decomposition breaks strong covalent O-H bonds and forms new substances.
choices.rationale: Correct: 44 kJ/mol is the scale of intermolecular attractions (hydrogen bonds); 242 kJ/mol is the scale of covalent bond energies.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Decomposition needs more energy because the molecules in a gas are farther apart than in a liquid.
choices.rationale: The distance between molecules in the gas is the result of vaporization and does not make decomposition cost energy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Decomposition must also overcome the hydrogen bonds in the liquid, so it needs the vaporization energy plus extra energy.
choices.rationale: The decomposition data begin with H2O(g), where molecules are already separated, so hydrogen bonds in the liquid are not involved.

title: use energy data to tell breaking intermolecular forces from breaking covalent bonds (variant 1)
stem: The energy needed to sublime 1 mol of CO2(s) is about 25 kJ. The energy needed to decompose 1 mol of CO2(g) into C(s) and O2(g) is about 394 kJ. Which statement best interprets these data?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sublimation breaks C=O bonds in each molecule, but fewer of them than decomposition.
choices.rationale: Sublimed CO2 is still CO2, so no C=O bonds in the molecules were broken.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decomposition needs more energy because solid CO2 has stronger intermolecular forces than gaseous CO2.
choices.rationale: Decomposition starts from gaseous CO2, where the intermolecular forces are negligible, so this does not explain the energy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both processes break covalent bonds, and the difference is only in how many bonds break.
choices.rationale: Sublimation breaks no covalent bonds, and only the decomposition does so.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sublimation overcomes weak attractions between intact CO2 molecules, but decomposition breaks the C=O bonds within molecules.
choices.rationale: Correct: 25 kJ/mol corresponds to dispersion forces between molecules; 394 kJ/mol corresponds to breaking strong double bonds.

title: use energy data to tell breaking intermolecular forces from breaking covalent bonds (variant 2)
stem: The energy needed to melt 1 mol of NaCl(s) is about 28 kJ. The energy needed to convert 1 mol of NaCl(s) into Na(s) and 1/2 Cl2(g) is about 411 kJ. Which statement best interprets these data?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Melting converts Na⁺ ions to Na atoms, but only partly, so less energy is needed than for complete conversion.
choices.rationale: Melting does not change any ions into atoms; the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are still present in the liquid.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Melting loosens the lattice but leaves Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in the same substance, while the second process changes the ions into Na atoms and Cl2 molecules.
choices.rationale: Correct: molten NaCl is still NaCl made of Na⁺ and Cl⁻, a physical change; producing Na(s) and Cl2(g) is a chemical change requiring electron transfer.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both processes produce new substances, and the larger energy change is due to producing a gas.
choices.rationale: Melting does not produce a new substance, so it is a physical change.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Melting breaks every ionic bond completely, so the second process must be breaking something else, such as nuclei.
choices.rationale: Nuclei are never broken in chemical processes, and melting does not completely separate the ions, which still attract each other in the liquid.

title: use energy data to tell breaking intermolecular forces from breaking covalent bonds (variant 3)
stem: The energy needed to sublime 1 mol of I2(s) is about 62 kJ. The energy needed to dissociate 1 mol of I2(g) into 2 I(g) is about 151 kJ. Which statement best interprets these data?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sublimation is a chemical change because it needs a large amount of energy.
choices.rationale: The size of the energy alone does not define a chemical change; sublimation gives the same I2 molecules in the gas phase.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sublimation overcomes dispersion forces between intact I2 molecules, while dissociation breaks the I-I covalent bond and forms different particles.
choices.rationale: Correct: sublimation gives I2 molecules in the gas phase; dissociation gives I atoms, a different species.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both processes break I-I bonds, and dissociation requires more energy because the bonds are stronger in the gas.
choices.rationale: Sublimation leaves the I-I bonds intact, and the molecules just separate.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dissociation is a physical change because the iodine remains iodine.
choices.rationale: The I atoms have different properties from I2 molecules, and the covalent bond is broken, so it is a chemical change.

title: find the limiting reactant from masses, then compute percent yield
stem: Aluminum reacts with chlorine according to 2 Al + 3 Cl2 → 2 AlCl3. A student mixes 5.40 g of Al (26.98 g/mol) with 10.65 g of Cl2 (70.90 g/mol) and collects 11.2 g of AlCl3 (133.33 g/mol). What is the percent yield?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: It uses Al as the limiting reactant (theoretical yield 26.7 g), but Cl2 runs out first.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct: 5.40 g Al = 0.2001 mol; 10.65 g Cl2 = 0.1502 mol; the Al would need 0.3002 mol Cl2, so Cl2 is limiting. AlCl3 = 0.1502 × 2/3 = 0.1001 mol = 13.35 g; 11.2 ÷ 13.35 = 83.9%.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: It uses the correct limiting reactant but a 1:1 mole ratio of Cl2 to AlCl3, giving 20.0 g as the theoretical yield.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: It uses the total mass of the reactants, 16.05 g, as the theoretical yield, which ignores the mole ratio and the limiting reactant.

title: find the limiting reactant from masses, then compute percent yield (variant 1)
stem: Ammonia reacts with oxygen according to 4 NH3 + 5 O2 → 4 NO + 6 H2O. A student mixes 8.50 g of NH3 (17.03 g/mol) with 16.0 g of O2 (32.00 g/mol) and collects 9.60 g of NO (30.01 g/mol). What is the percent yield?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Correct: 8.50 g NH3 = 0.4991 mol; 16.0 g O2 = 0.5000 mol; NH3 would need 0.624 mol O2, so O2 is limiting. NO = 0.5000 × 4/5 = 0.4000 mol = 12.0 g; 9.60 ÷ 12.0 = 80.0%.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: It takes NH3 as the limiting reactant (theoretical yield 14.98 g), but O2 runs out first.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: It multiplies the moles of O2 by 5/4 instead of 4/5, inverting the mole ratio.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: It divides by the total mass of the reactants, which ignores stoichiometry.

title: find the limiting reactant from masses, then compute percent yield (variant 2)
stem: In the thermite reaction Fe2O3 + 2 Al → Al2O3 + 2 Fe, a student mixes 16.0 g of Fe2O3 (159.69 g/mol) with 4.05 g of Al (26.98 g/mol) and obtains 6.70 g of Fe (55.85 g/mol). What is the percent yield of iron?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: It divides by the total mass of the two reactants, 20.05 g, which has nothing to do with the iron that can form.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: It takes Fe2O3 as limiting and counts 2 Fe per Fe2O3 (11.19 g), but Al runs out first.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: It doubles the moles of Fe formed from the Al, using 2 Fe per Al, which inverts the 1:1 mole ratio.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Correct: 16.0 g Fe2O3 = 0.1002 mol; 4.05 g Al = 0.1501 mol; Fe2O3 would need 0.2004 mol Al, so Al is limiting. Fe = 0.1501 mol = 8.38 g; 6.70 ÷ 8.38 = 79.9%.

title: find the limiting reactant from masses, then compute percent yield (variant 3)
stem: Hydrogen burns in oxygen according to 2 H2 + O2 → 2 H2O. A student mixes 3.00 g of H2 (2.016 g/mol) with 20.0 g of O2 (32.00 g/mol) and collects 19.4 g of H2O (18.02 g/mol). What is the percent yield?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Correct: 3.00 g H2 = 1.488 mol; 20.0 g O2 = 0.625 mol; The O2 needs 1.250 mol H2 and 1.488 mol H2 is available, so O2 is limiting. H2O = 1.250 mol = 22.5 g; 19.4 ÷ 22.5 = 86.1%.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: It takes H2 as the limiting reactant (26.8 g of water), but O2 runs out first.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: It compares the mass of water with the mass of O2 only, which ignores the mole ratio.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: It compares the product with the total mass of the reactants, 23.0 g, which ignores the limiting reactant and the mole ratio.

title: use a product's mass and the mole ratio to find the purity of a reactant
stem: An impure 5.00 g sample of KClO3 (122.55 g/mol) is heated until it decomposes completely according to 2 KClO3 → 2 KCl + 3 O2. The impurities do not release any gas. The O2 produced has a mass of 1.20 g (32.00 g/mol). What is the mass percent of KClO3 in the sample?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: It uses a 1:1 mole ratio between O2 and KClO3, but 3 O2 form per 2 KClO3.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: It ignores the coefficient 2 on KClO3 and uses 1 KClO3 per 3 O2, which halves the answer.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: It divides the mass of O2 by the mass of the sample, which skips the conversion through moles and the mole ratio.

title: use a product's mass and the mole ratio to find the purity of a reactant (variant 1)
stem: An impure 2.25 g sample of aluminum reacts with excess HCl according to 2 Al + 6 HCl → 2 AlCl3 + 3 H2. The impurities do not react. The H2 produced has a mass of 0.150 g (2.016 g/mol). What is the mass percent of Al (26.98 g/mol) in the sample?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: It uses a 1:1 mole ratio of Al to H2, but 3 H2 form per 2 Al.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: It divides the mass of H2 by the mass of the sample, which skips the mole conversion.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: It uses 1 Al per 3 H2, forgetting the coefficient 2 on Al.

title: use a product's mass and the mole ratio to find the purity of a reactant (variant 2)
stem: An impure 4.20 g sample of NaHCO3 (84.01 g/mol) is heated according to 2 NaHCO3 → Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2. The impurities do not release gas. The CO2 produced has a mass of 0.880 g (44.01 g/mol). What is the mass percent of NaHCO3 in the sample?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: It uses a 1:1 mole ratio, but 2 NaHCO3 form each CO2.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: It divides the mass of CO2 by the mass of the sample, skipping the moles and the mole ratio.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: It inverts the ratio, using 1 NaHCO3 per 2 CO2, which gives 0.84 g.

title: use a product's mass and the mole ratio to find the purity of a reactant (variant 3)
stem: Hydrogen peroxide solution decomposes according to 2 H2O2 → 2 H2O + O2. A 10.00 g sample of the solution produces 0.141 g of O2 (32.00 g/mol). What is the mass percent of H2O2 (34.01 g/mol) in the solution?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: It divides the mass of O2 by the mass of the sample and skips the mole conversion.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: It applies the 2:1 ratio twice, which doubles the correct moles of H2O2.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: It uses a 1:1 ratio between H2O2 and O2, but 2 H2O2 form each O2.

title: find an unknown concentration from titration volumes when the mole ratio is not 1:1
stem: A 25.00 mL sample of H2SO4(aq) is titrated to the equivalence point with 0.2000 M NaOH(aq), which requires 30.00 mL. The reaction is H2SO4 + 2 NaOH → Na2SO4 + 2 H2O. What is the concentration of the H2SO4 solution?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: It assumes a 1:1 mole ratio, but each H2SO4 needs two NaOH.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: It divides by the total volume of the mixture, 55.00 mL, instead of the 25.00 mL acid sample.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: It inverts the volume ratio, calculating 0.2000 × 25.00 ÷ 30.00 and then halving.

title: find an unknown concentration from titration volumes when the mole ratio is not 1:1 (variant 1)
stem: A 20.00 mL sample of Ba(OH)2(aq) is titrated to the equivalence point with 0.1500 M HCl(aq), which requires 28.40 mL. The reaction is Ba(OH)2 + 2 HCl → BaCl2 + 2 H2O. What is the concentration of the Ba(OH)2 solution?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: It assumes 1:1 stoichiometry and does not halve the moles of acid.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: It divides by 2 a second time after already using the 1:2 ratio.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: It divides by the total volume, 48.40 mL, instead of the 20.00 mL of base.

title: find an unknown concentration from titration volumes when the mole ratio is not 1:1 (variant 2)
stem: A 25.00 mL sample of H3PO4(aq) is titrated with 0.1000 M NaOH(aq) until both of the first two protons have been neutralized, forming Na2HPO4. This requires 37.50 mL of NaOH. What is the concentration of the H3PO4 solution?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: It uses a 1:1 mole ratio of NaOH to H3PO4, which ignores that two protons react.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: It uses 3 NaOH per H3PO4, but the titration stops after two protons.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Correct: mol NaOH = 0.1000 × 0.03750 = 3.750 × 10⁻³ mol; H3PO4 reacts with 2 NaOH to form Na2HPO4, so mol H3PO4 = 1.875 × 10⁻³ mol; M = 1.875 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.02500 = 0.0750 M.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: It multiplies by the number of protons instead of dividing.

title: find an unknown concentration from titration volumes when the mole ratio is not 1:1 (variant 3)
stem: A 10.00 mL sample of vinegar is diluted to 100.0 mL with water. A 25.00 mL portion of the diluted solution is titrated to the equivalence point with 0.1000 M NaOH, which requires 21.40 mL. The reaction is HC2H3O2 + NaOH → NaC2H3O2 + H2O. What is the concentration of acetic acid in the original, undiluted vinegar?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: It gives the concentration of the diluted solution and forgets to correct for the dilution.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: It divides the moles by 10.00 mL, the volume of vinegar, instead of the 25.00 mL titrated.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: It multiplies by 100, using the final volume instead of the dilution factor of 10.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Correct: mol NaOH = 0.1000 × 0.02140 = 2.140 × 10⁻³ mol = mol acid in the 25.00 mL portion; diluted M = 0.0856; the dilution factor is 10, so the vinegar is 0.856 M.

title: predict how a procedural error changes a calculated concentration
stem: A student titrates 25.00 mL of HCl of unknown concentration with standard 0.100 M NaOH from a buret. Before filling, the student rinses the buret with distilled water and leaves the water droplets in it. The titration is otherwise done correctly, and the equivalence point is detected correctly. The student calculates the HCl concentration using 0.100 M for the NaOH. How will the calculated HCl concentration compare with the true value?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It will be too low, because the water neutralizes some of the acid.
choices.rationale: Water is neutral and neutralizes nothing; its effect is to dilute the base.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It will be correct, because water does not contain any acid or base.
choices.rationale: Water does not add acid or base, but it lowers the concentration of the NaOH, and that changes the result.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It will be too high, because the diluted NaOH has a lower concentration than 0.100 M, so more volume is needed and the calculation overestimates the moles of base.
choices.rationale: Correct: water in the buret dilutes the NaOH, so the actual concentration is below 0.100 M. More volume is needed, and calculating with 0.100 M overestimates the moles of NaOH and so the HCl concentration.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It will be too low, because less NaOH is needed to reach the equivalence point.
choices.rationale: A diluted base requires more volume, not less, to supply the same number of moles.

title: predict how a procedural error changes a calculated concentration (variant 1)
stem: A student titrates 25.00 mL of HCl with 0.100 M NaOH. The tip of the buret contains an air bubble before the titration, and the bubble is expelled during the titration. The initial buret reading is taken with the bubble present. How will the calculated HCl concentration compare with the true value?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It will be too low, because the bubble reduces the volume of NaOH delivered.
choices.rationale: The recorded volume is larger than the real volume delivered, so the calculation overestimates the base.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It will be too high, because the volume difference read from the buret includes the volume the bubble occupied, which is more than the liquid delivered.
choices.rationale: Correct: the buret reading falls by the volume of liquid delivered plus the volume of liquid that replaces the bubble, so the recorded volume of NaOH is larger than the volume that reacted; the calculation overestimates the moles of base, so the HCl concentration comes out too high.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It will be correct, because the bubble contains no NaOH and does not change the reaction.
choices.rationale: The bubble does not change the reaction, but it changes the volume that is recorded.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It will be too low, because the bubble makes the endpoint appear earlier.
choices.rationale: A bubble does not change when the indicator turns color; it only changes the volume reading.

title: predict how a procedural error changes a calculated concentration (variant 2)
stem: A student pipets 25.00 mL of HCl into a flask that was rinsed with distilled water and is still wet. The student then titrates with standardized 0.100 M NaOH, using phenolphthalein. How will the calculated HCl concentration compare with the true value?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It will be too low, because the added water dilutes the acid.
choices.rationale: Dilution lowers the concentration in the flask, but the moles of acid do not change, and the calculation uses the pipetted volume and moles.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It will be too high, because more NaOH is needed to neutralize the water.
choices.rationale: Water is neutral and needs no base, so the volume of NaOH is set by the moles of HCl.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It will be too low, because the water makes the indicator change color early.
choices.rationale: Water does not change the pH at which phenolphthalein changes color.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It will be correct, because the water changes the concentration but not the moles of HCl, and the moles are what the NaOH neutralizes.
choices.rationale: Correct: the moles of HCl in the flask are fixed by the pipet, so the volume of NaOH needed does not change.

title: predict how a procedural error changes a calculated concentration (variant 3)
stem: A student rinses the pipet with distilled water and does not rinse it with the HCl sample before pipetting 25.00 mL of the HCl for titration with 0.100 M NaOH. How will the calculated HCl concentration compare with the true value?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It will be too high, because the water adds volume that needs to be neutralized.
choices.rationale: Water is neutral and has nothing to neutralize; the effect of the dilution is fewer moles of acid in the pipetted volume.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It will be correct, because the pipet still delivers 25.00 mL.
choices.rationale: The volume is correct, but its concentration is lower than that of the original sample, so the moles are lower.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It will be too low, because the sample in the pipet is diluted by the water, so it delivers fewer moles of HCl and requires less NaOH.
choices.rationale: Correct: water left in the pipet dilutes the sample, so the 25.00 mL contains fewer moles than expected. Less NaOH is needed, but the calculation still divides by 25.00 mL, so the calculated concentration is too low.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It will be too high, because the extra water increases the pH at the equivalence point.
choices.rationale: The added water does not change the equivalence point pH of a strong acid-strong base titration, and it does not make the calculation higher.

title: classify a reaction from an observation and decide whether electrons are transferred
stem: A zinc strip is placed in blue CuSO4(aq). Over time, the strip becomes coated with a reddish-brown solid and the blue color fades. Which classification best describes the reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Synthesis, because zinc and copper combine into one product.
choices.rationale: No single product forms; Zn²⁺ stays in solution and copper metal forms separately.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Double replacement, because the ions swap partners to form an insoluble solid.
choices.rationale: The solid is copper metal, which is an element and not an ionic precipitate, and electrons are transferred.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Single replacement and redox, because Zn loses electrons and Cu²⁺ gains them to form Cu(s).
choices.rationale: Correct: Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu. Zn goes 0 → +2 and Cu goes +2 → 0, so the reaction is redox, and the metal replaces a metal ion in solution.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Decomposition, because the blue CuSO4 breaks down into simpler substances.
choices.rationale: The reaction has two reactants, and the sulfate ion does not change; the copper is replaced by zinc.

title: classify a reaction from an observation and decide whether electrons are transferred (variant 1)
stem: Colorless Na2CO3(aq) is mixed with colorless CaCl2(aq). A cloudy white solid forms, with no gas, no flame and no color change, and no element changes its oxidation number. Which classification best describes the reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Double replacement (precipitation), which is not a redox reaction.
choices.rationale: Correct: Ca²⁺ + CO3²⁻ → CaCO3(s); oxidation numbers are unchanged, so it is not redox.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Single replacement, because Ca replaces Na in the compound.
choices.rationale: Both cations and anions exchange partners, and no free element is involved, so it is double replacement.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Combustion, because a new substance forms and energy is released.
choices.rationale: Combustion needs oxygen as a reactant, and none is involved here.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Single replacement and redox, because a solid forms.
choices.rationale: A solid forming does not indicate electron transfer, and no oxidation numbers change.

title: classify a reaction from an observation and decide whether electrons are transferred (variant 2)
stem: A white solid is heated and releases a gas that relights a glowing splint. The solid left behind is KCl. The reaction is 2 KClO3 → 2 KCl + 3 O2. Which classification is best?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Synthesis, because a gas is formed.
choices.rationale: Synthesis combines several reactants into one product, and here one reactant forms two products.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decomposition, but not redox, because only one reactant is involved.
choices.rationale: The number of reactants does not decide whether a reaction is redox; the oxidation numbers of Cl and O change.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Decomposition and redox, because Cl goes from +5 to -1 and O goes from -2 to 0.
choices.rationale: Correct: Cl is +5 in KClO3 and -1 in KCl; O is -2 in KClO3 and 0 in O2; one reactant gives several products.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Single replacement, because chlorine is replaced by oxygen.
choices.rationale: There is only one reactant, so nothing replaces anything else.

title: classify a reaction from an observation and decide whether electrons are transferred (variant 3)
stem: Magnesium ribbon is added to dilute HCl(aq). Bubbles of H2 gas form and the ribbon disappears. Which classification best describes the reaction Mg + 2 HCl → MgCl2 + H2?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acid-base neutralization, because HCl is an acid.
choices.rationale: A neutralization is a proton transfer to a base such as OH⁻, but Mg is a metal that transfers electrons.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Single replacement and redox, because Mg is oxidized and H⁺ is reduced.
choices.rationale: Correct: Mg goes 0 → +2 (oxidized); H goes +1 → 0 (reduced); a free element replaces another element in a compound.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Double replacement, because Mg²⁺ and H⁺ swap anions.
choices.rationale: A free element (Mg) reacts, so a double replacement does not apply.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Decomposition, because HCl breaks down into H2.
choices.rationale: There are two reactants, and the Cl stays as Cl⁻ in MgCl2.

title: combine reaction-type patterns with oxidation numbers to see that type does not decide redox
stem: Which reaction is a synthesis (combination) reaction that is NOT an oxidation-reduction reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 2 Mg + O2 → 2 MgO
choices.rationale: It is a synthesis, but Mg goes from 0 to +2 and O goes from 0 to -2, so it is redox.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: It is a decomposition and redox because O in H2O2 (-1) changes to -2 and 0.

choices.label: C
choices.text: CaO + CO2 → CaCO3
choices.rationale: Correct: in CaO + CO2 → CaCO3, Ca stays +2, C stays +4 and O stays -2; two reactants form one product.

choices.label: D
choices.text: CaCO3 → CaO + CO2
choices.rationale: It is a decomposition, not a synthesis, although no oxidation numbers change.

title: combine reaction-type patterns with oxidation numbers to see that type does not decide redox (variant 1)
stem: Which reaction is a decomposition reaction that is also an oxidation-reduction reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CaCO3 → CaO + CO2
choices.rationale: It is a decomposition, but Ca, C and O keep the same oxidation numbers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mg(OH)2 → MgO + H2O
choices.rationale: It is a decomposition, but no oxidation number changes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 2 KClO3 → 2 KCl + 3 O2
choices.rationale: Correct: only in KClO3 → KCl + O2 do oxidation numbers change (Cl +5 → -1, O -2 → 0).

choices.label: D
choices.text: NH4Cl → NH3 + HCl
choices.rationale: It is a decomposition, but N stays -3, H stays +1 and Cl stays -1.

title: combine reaction-type patterns with oxidation numbers to see that type does not decide redox (variant 2)
stem: Which reaction is a synthesis reaction that is also an oxidation-reduction reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: SO3 + H2O → H2SO4
choices.rationale: It is a synthesis, but S stays +6, O stays -2 and H stays +1.

choices.label: B
choices.text: NH3 + HCl → NH4Cl
choices.rationale: It is a synthesis in which a proton transfers, but no oxidation numbers change.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Na2O + H2O → 2 NaOH
choices.rationale: It is a synthesis in which no element changes its oxidation number.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Correct: in N2 + 3 H2 → 2 NH3, N goes 0 → -3 and H goes 0 → +1; in the others no oxidation numbers change.

title: combine reaction-type patterns with oxidation numbers to see that type does not decide redox (variant 3)
stem: Which reaction is NOT an oxidation-reduction reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cl2 + 2 KBr → 2 KCl + Br2
choices.rationale: Cl goes 0 → -1 and Br goes -1 → 0, so it is redox.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fe + CuSO4 → FeSO4 + Cu
choices.rationale: Fe goes 0 → +2 and Cu goes +2 → 0, so it is redox.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mg + 2 HCl → MgCl2 + H2
choices.rationale: Mg goes 0 → +2 and H goes +1 → 0, so it is redox.

choices.label: D
choices.text: BaCl2 + Na2SO4 → BaSO4 + 2 NaCl
choices.rationale: Correct: in the precipitation reaction all ions keep their charges (Ba +2, Cl -1, Na +1, SO4 -2).

title: recognize an amphiprotic species as an acid with a base and a base with an acid
stem: Consider the reactions of hydrogencarbonate ion, HCO3⁻, with aqueous NaOH and with aqueous HCl. Which statement correctly describes the role of HCO3⁻ in these reactions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is an acid in both reactions, because it contains a hydrogen atom.
choices.rationale: An ion acts as an acid only if it can give a proton to a base, and with H3O⁺ it accepts one instead.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It acts as an acid with OH⁻ (donating H⁺ to form CO3²⁻) and as a base with H3O⁺ (accepting H⁺ to form H2CO3).
choices.rationale: Correct: HCO3⁻ + OH⁻ → CO3²⁻ + H2O (donates H⁺); HCO3⁻ + H3O⁺ → H2CO3 + H2O (accepts H⁺).

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a base in both reactions, because it carries a negative charge.
choices.rationale: Charge does not decide the role; HCO3⁻ can still donate its H⁺ to a strong base like OH⁻.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It acts as a base with OH⁻ (accepting H⁺) and as an acid with H3O⁺ (donating H⁺).
choices.rationale: OH⁻ has no H⁺ to give to HCO3⁻, so HCO3⁻ cannot accept a proton from it, and H3O⁺ is a proton donor.

title: recognize an amphiprotic species as an acid with a base and a base with an acid (variant 1)
stem: Which pair gives the products formed when HPO4²⁻ reacts with OH⁻ and with H3O⁺, respectively?

choices.label: A
choices.text: H2PO4⁻ with OH⁻, and PO4³⁻ with H3O⁺
choices.rationale: It reverses the roles; OH⁻ takes H⁺ from the ion, and H3O⁺ gives H⁺ to it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: H2PO4⁻ with both OH⁻ and H3O⁺
choices.rationale: HPO4²⁻ cannot accept a proton from OH⁻, so H2PO4⁻ cannot form with it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: PO4³⁻ with OH⁻, and H3PO4 with H3O⁺
choices.rationale: A single reaction with H3O⁺ transfers one proton, giving H2PO4⁻, and not two protons giving H3PO4.

choices.label: D
choices.text: PO4³⁻ with OH⁻, and H2PO4⁻ with H3O⁺
choices.rationale: Correct: with OH⁻, HPO4²⁻ donates H⁺ → PO4³⁻ + H2O; with H3O⁺, it accepts one H⁺ → H2PO4⁻ + H2O.

title: recognize an amphiprotic species as an acid with a base and a base with an acid (variant 2)
stem: Water reacts with NH3 and, separately, with HF. Which statement correctly describes the role of H2O in these two reactions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is an acid with NH3 (forming NH4⁺ and OH⁻) and a base with HF (forming H3O⁺ and F⁻).
choices.rationale: Correct: NH3 + H2O ⇌ NH4⁺ + OH⁻ (H2O donates H⁺); HF + H2O ⇌ H3O⁺ + F⁻ (H2O accepts H⁺).

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a base with NH3 and an acid with HF.
choices.rationale: This reverses the roles; NH3 is a base and accepts H⁺ from water, and HF donates H⁺ to water.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is an acid in both reactions, because it contains hydrogen.
choices.rationale: In the reaction with HF, water accepts a proton to form H3O⁺, so it is a base there.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is neither, because water is neutral and does not transfer protons.
choices.rationale: A neutral molecule can still donate or accept protons, and water is amphiprotic.

title: recognize an amphiprotic species as an acid with a base and a base with an acid (variant 3)
stem: In the reaction HS⁻ + NH4⁺ → H2S + NH3, which two pairs are the conjugate acid-base pairs?

choices.label: A
choices.text: HS⁻ / NH4⁺ and H2S / NH3
choices.rationale: These pair species from opposite sides of the proton transfer, but a conjugate pair differs by only one H⁺.

choices.label: B
choices.text: HS⁻ / NH3 and H2S / NH4⁺
choices.rationale: HS⁻ and NH3 do not differ by a proton, so they are not a pair.

choices.label: C
choices.text: H2S / HS⁻ and NH4⁺ / NH3
choices.rationale: Correct: NH4⁺ donates H⁺ to HS⁻, so the pairs differ by one H⁺: NH4⁺ / NH3 and H2S / HS⁻.

choices.label: D
choices.text: H2S / S²⁻ and NH4⁺ / NH3
choices.rationale: S²⁻ does not appear in the reaction; the conjugate base of H2S here is HS⁻.

title: separate acid strength from the amount of base needed for neutralization
stem: Two flasks each contain 25.0 mL of 0.100 M acid. Flask 1 holds HCl, a strong acid, and flask 2 holds CH3COOH, a weak acid. Each is titrated with 0.100 M NaOH to its equivalence point. Which statement compares the volumes of NaOH required?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both need 25.0 mL, because the flasks contain equal moles of acid, and the un-ionized CH3COOH reacts as the NaOH removes the H⁺ that has formed.
choices.rationale: Correct: each flask contains 0.0250 L × 0.100 M = 2.50 mmol of acid, and each acid reacts 1:1 with NaOH, so each needs 25.0 mL.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Flask 1 needs more NaOH, because HCl produces more H⁺ in solution.
choices.rationale: Strength tells the degree of ionization, not the total number of acidic protons available for neutralization.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Flask 2 needs less NaOH, because only the small fraction of CH3COOH that is ionized can be neutralized.
choices.rationale: As OH⁻ removes H⁺, more CH3COOH ionizes (Le Chatelier), so all of it is eventually neutralized.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Flask 2 needs more NaOH, because a weak acid is harder to neutralize.
choices.rationale: A weak acid has a different pH profile, but neutralization needs the same moles of OH⁻ for the same moles of acid.

title: separate acid strength from the amount of base needed for neutralization (variant 1)
stem: Which sample requires more 0.100 M NaOH to reach its equivalence point: 100.0 mL of 0.100 M HCl or 50.0 mL of 0.300 M CH3COOH?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The CH3COOH, because it contains 15.0 mmol of acid and the HCl contains only 10.0 mmol.
choices.rationale: Correct: HCl: 100.0 mL × 0.100 M = 10.0 mmol; CH3COOH: 50.0 mL × 0.300 M = 15.0 mmol; each is monoprotic, so CH3COOH needs 150 mL and HCl needs 100 mL.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The HCl, because it is a strong acid.
choices.rationale: Strong acids are not neutralized with more base; the moles of acid decide.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both need the same volume, because each acid reacts 1:1 with NaOH.
choices.rationale: The 1:1 ratio is true, but the two samples contain different moles of acid.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The HCl, because its volume is larger.
choices.rationale: Volume alone does not decide it, since concentration matters, and the product gives the moles.

title: separate acid strength from the amount of base needed for neutralization (variant 2)
stem: Two 25.0 mL samples, one of 0.100 M HCl and one of 0.100 M H2SO4, are each titrated with 0.100 M NaOH until both acidic protons of each acid are neutralized. Which statement compares the volumes of NaOH required?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are equal, because the acids have the same concentration and volume.
choices.rationale: Equal concentration does not mean equal moles of H⁺, because H2SO4 is diprotic.

choices.label: B
choices.text: H2SO4 needs twice as much, because each H2SO4 supplies two H⁺ to be neutralized.
choices.rationale: Correct: HCl: 2.50 mmol → 25.0 mL; H2SO4: 2.50 mmol × 2 = 5.00 mmol H⁺ → 50.0 mL.

choices.label: C
choices.text: HCl needs twice as much, because it is the stronger acid.
choices.rationale: Acid strength does not change the amount of base needed for complete neutralization.

choices.label: D
choices.text: H2SO4 needs 1.5 times as much, because its second H⁺ is only partly ionized.
choices.rationale: The second proton of H2SO4 is neutralized by the NaOH as well as the first, so the factor is 2 and not 1.5.

title: separate acid strength from the amount of base needed for neutralization (variant 3)
stem: A student titrates 20.0 mL of 0.150 M HBr (a strong acid) and, separately, 20.0 mL of 0.150 M HF (a weak acid, Ka = 6.8 × 10⁻⁴) with 0.100 M KOH. What volume of KOH is needed to reach the equivalence point in each titration?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 30.0 mL for each acid
choices.rationale: Correct: each flask has 20.0 mL × 0.150 M = 3.00 mmol of monoprotic acid; V = 3.00 mmol ÷ 0.100 M = 30.0 mL.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 30.0 mL for HBr and less than 30.0 mL for HF
choices.rationale: HF is only partly ionized, but its un-ionized molecules still react with OH⁻, so none of the acid is left unneutralized.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 30.0 mL for HBr and more than 30.0 mL for HF
choices.rationale: Weak acid strength does not require extra KOH, since the stoichiometry is 1:1.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 15.0 mL for each acid
choices.rationale: It halves the volume, as though each acid supplied one half mole of H⁺ per mole.

title: assign oxidation numbers to find what is oxidized, what is reduced, and electrons transferred
stem: In the reaction 2 Al(s) + Fe2O3(s) → Al2O3(s) + 2 Fe(s), which statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Al is the oxidizing agent because it is oxidized.
choices.rationale: The species that is oxidized is the reducing agent; the oxidizing agent is the species that is reduced.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fe2O3 is the reducing agent because the iron in it is reduced.
choices.rationale: The species that is reduced is the oxidizing agent and takes electrons from Al.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fe2O3 is the oxidizing agent: each Fe goes from +3 to 0, and 6 electrons are transferred per Fe2O3.
choices.rationale: Correct: Al 0 → +3 (oxidized, reducing agent), Fe +3 → 0 (reduced, oxidizing agent), O is -2 on both sides. Two Fe gain 3 e⁻ each, so 6 e⁻ are transferred.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oxygen is oxidized, since it goes from -2 in Fe2O3 to 0 in Al2O3.
choices.rationale: Oxygen is -2 in both Fe2O3 and Al2O3, so its oxidation number does not change.

title: assign oxidation numbers to find what is oxidized, what is reduced, and electrons transferred (variant 1)
stem: In the reaction MnO4⁻ + 5 Fe²⁺ + 8 H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5 Fe³⁺ + 4 H2O, how many electrons does each MnO4⁻ gain, and which species is the reducing agent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 5 electrons; Fe²⁺ is the reducing agent
choices.rationale: Correct: Mn goes +7 → +2, a gain of 5 e⁻; each Fe²⁺ loses 1 e⁻ to become Fe³⁺, so Fe²⁺ is the reducing agent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 7 electrons; MnO4⁻ is the reducing agent
choices.rationale: The oxidation number of Mn in MnO4⁻ is +7, but its change is 5, and MnO4⁻ is the oxidizing agent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 5 electrons; MnO4⁻ is the reducing agent
choices.rationale: The number 5 is correct, but MnO4⁻ is reduced and so is the oxidizing agent.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 7 electrons; Fe²⁺ is the reducing agent
choices.rationale: Fe²⁺ is the reducing agent, but 7 is the oxidation number of Mn, and not the number of electrons gained.

title: assign oxidation numbers to find what is oxidized, what is reduced, and electrons transferred (variant 2)
stem: In the reaction CuO(s) + H2(g) → Cu(s) + H2O(g), which statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: H2 is reduced and is the oxidizing agent.
choices.rationale: H2 goes from 0 to +1, so it is oxidized and it is the reducing agent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cu²⁺ in CuO is reduced, and H2 is the reducing agent.
choices.rationale: Correct: Cu +2 → 0 (reduced); H 0 → +1 (oxidized); O is -2 on both sides.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oxygen is reduced from -2 to 0.
choices.rationale: Oxygen is -2 in both CuO and H2O, and it is unchanged.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cu is oxidized from 0 to +2.
choices.rationale: This reverses the reaction; in this reaction Cu goes from +2 to 0.

title: assign oxidation numbers to find what is oxidized, what is reduced, and electrons transferred (variant 3)
stem: In the reaction Zn(s) + 2 Ag⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2 Ag(s), how many electrons are transferred as the equation is written, and which species is the oxidizing agent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 2 electrons; Ag⁺ is the oxidizing agent
choices.rationale: Correct: Zn 0 → +2 loses 2 e⁻; each of 2 Ag⁺ gains 1 e⁻, so 2 e⁻ are transferred in total; Ag⁺ is reduced and so is the oxidizing agent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 2 electrons; Zn is the oxidizing agent
choices.rationale: Zn is oxidized, so it is the reducing agent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 1 electron; Ag⁺ is the oxidizing agent
choices.rationale: One electron is gained per Ag⁺, but the equation has 2 Ag⁺, so 2 electrons are transferred.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 4 electrons; Zn is the oxidizing agent
choices.rationale: It adds the electrons lost and gained, but the same 2 electrons are lost by Zn and gained by Ag⁺, so counting them twice is incorrect.

title: recognize disproportionation, where one species is both oxidized and reduced
stem: In the reaction 2 H2O2(aq) → 2 H2O(l) + O2(g), which statement about oxidation numbers is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hydrogen is oxidized from +1 to 0.
choices.rationale: Hydrogen is +1 in both H2O2 and H2O, and no hydrogen gas forms.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oxygen in H2O2 is -1; it is reduced to -2 in H2O and oxidized to 0 in O2, so H2O2 is both oxidized and reduced.
choices.rationale: Correct: H is +1 throughout; O is -1 in H2O2, -2 in H2O and 0 in O2.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oxygen is -2 in H2O2 and is only oxidized to 0 in O2, so H2O2 is only a reducing agent.
choices.rationale: In H2O2 the oxygen is -1 (the peroxide ion has two O atoms sharing a charge of -2), and it also forms H2O at -2.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is not a redox reaction, because only one reactant is present.
choices.rationale: The number of reactants does not decide whether a reaction is redox; oxidation numbers change here.

title: recognize disproportionation, where one species is both oxidized and reduced (variant 1)
stem: In the reaction Cl2(g) + 2 NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + NaOCl(aq) + H2O(l), which statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chlorine is only reduced, because it forms the chloride ion.
choices.rationale: Some of the chlorine also ends up as +1 in NaOCl, so it is oxidized as well.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sodium is oxidized, because it appears in both products.
choices.rationale: Na is +1 on both sides, so it does not change.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oxygen is oxidized, because it goes from -2 in OH⁻ to -1 in NaOCl.
choices.rationale: O is -2 in both OH⁻ and OCl⁻, because the chlorine is the element whose oxidation number is changing.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Chlorine is both oxidized and reduced, going from 0 in Cl2 to -1 in NaCl and +1 in NaOCl.
choices.rationale: Correct: Cl 0 → -1 (reduced) and Cl 0 → +1 (oxidized); Na stays +1; O stays -2 and H stays +1.

title: recognize disproportionation, where one species is both oxidized and reduced (variant 2)
stem: In aqueous solution, copper(I) ions react according to 2 Cu⁺(aq) → Cu(s) + Cu²⁺(aq). Which statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is not a redox reaction, because Cu appears on both sides of the equation.
choices.rationale: The oxidation numbers of copper differ in the three species, so the reaction is redox.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cu⁺ is only reduced, because copper metal forms.
choices.rationale: Some Cu⁺ ions are oxidized to Cu²⁺ as well.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two electrons are transferred from each Cu⁺ ion to a neighboring ion.
choices.rationale: Each Cu⁺ gains or loses only one electron, and 2 electrons are never transferred from a single ion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: One Cu⁺ is oxidized to Cu²⁺ and the other is reduced to Cu, so Cu⁺ is both the oxidizing and the reducing agent, with 1 electron transferred.
choices.rationale: Correct: Cu +1 → +2 (loses 1 e⁻) and Cu +1 → 0 (gains 1 e⁻); 1 electron is transferred in total.

title: recognize disproportionation, where one species is both oxidized and reduced (variant 3)
stem: In the reaction 3 NO2(g) + H2O(l) → 2 HNO3(aq) + NO(g), which statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Nitrogen is only oxidized, because HNO3 has more oxygen than NO2.
choices.rationale: Some nitrogen is also reduced to +2 in NO, and the change in oxygen content is not what defines oxidation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oxygen is reduced because it is -2 in NO2 and in NO.
choices.rationale: Oxygen is -2 in NO2, HNO3, NO and H2O, so it does not change.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nitrogen is +4 in NO2, is oxidized to +5 in HNO3 and is reduced to +2 in NO, so NO2 is both oxidized and reduced.
choices.rationale: Correct: N +4 → +5 (2 of the 3 N) and +4 → +2 (1 of the 3 N); electrons lost 2 × 1 = 2, gained 1 × 2 = 2. H (+1) and O (-2) do not change.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hydrogen is oxidized because it forms HNO3.
choices.rationale: Hydrogen is +1 in both H2O and HNO3, so its oxidation number does not change.
